title: The Case That Should Have Been Closed
content:
Inspector Daniel Mercer had learned, over twenty years of police work, that the most dangerous mistakes were rarely the obvious ones.

A broken window could be noticed.

A missing weapon could be reported.

A suspicious fingerprint could be investigated.

But an ordinary detail that nobody considered important could remain invisible for years.

That was why, when Daniel received an old case file on a cold Monday morning, he immediately noticed something that everyone else had overlooked.

The case had been closed twelve years earlier.

The victim, Arthur Bell, had been found dead in his study on the night of November 14. There had been no signs of forced entry, no weapon had been recovered, and no suspect had ever been formally charged.

The official conclusion had been suicide.

Daniel turned another page.

— Why was this reopened? — he asked.

Detective Clara Hughes placed a photograph on his desk.

— Because someone sent this to the station yesterday.

Daniel examined it.

It showed Arthur Bell's study exactly as it had appeared on the night of his death.

A desk.

A chair.

A fireplace.

A bookshelf.

And a large grandfather clock.

— What's wrong with it?

— Look at the clock.

Daniel looked again.

The clock showed 10:42.

— The report says Bell died shortly after eleven.

— Correct.

— So?

Clara pointed toward the fireplace.

— Look at the shadow.

Daniel leaned closer.

The photograph showed a long shadow extending across the carpet.

— What am I looking for?

— The clock wasn't standing there.

Daniel looked at her.

— What?

— The original crime-scene report says the clock was against the opposite wall.

He stared at the photograph again.

— Then someone moved it.

— Exactly.

Daniel opened the old report.

— Why isn't that mentioned?

— Because nobody noticed.

He closed the file slowly.

— Someone should have.

They returned to the Bell residence that afternoon.

The house had been renovated, but the study remained almost unchanged.

Daniel stood in the center of the room, comparing the photograph with the current layout.

— If the clock had been moved, there must have been a reason.

Clara walked toward the fireplace.

— Unless someone simply wanted to make the room look different.

— That's possible.

— Could have been an attempt to confuse the investigation.

Daniel nodded.

— It could have.

He examined the floor beneath the clock.

There were faint marks in the wooden boards.

— Someone moved it recently enough for the marks to remain visible when the photograph was taken.

Clara crouched beside him.

— Then whoever moved it was probably in a hurry.

Daniel looked at the old photograph again.

— Or they knew exactly what they were doing.

They searched the room carefully.

Behind the bookshelf, Clara discovered a small metal compartment.

Inside was a collection of letters.

Most concerned Arthur Bell's business affairs.

One, however, was different.

It had been written three days before his death.

Arthur,

You should have listened to me. If you continue investigating the accounts, you will put yourself in danger.

There was no signature.

Daniel read it twice.

— Someone was warning him.

— Or threatening him.

— Could have been both.

Clara looked at the letter.

— Who would have wanted him dead?

Daniel opened the financial records.

— Someone who had something to lose.

They spent the next two days investigating Bell's company.

Several irregular payments appeared in the records. Money had been transferred through multiple accounts before eventually disappearing.

One name appeared repeatedly.

Jonathan Reed.

Reed had been Bell's business partner.

He was now seventy-three and living outside the city.

When Daniel and Clara arrived at his house, he seemed unsurprised to see them.

— I wondered when someone would come asking about Arthur.

Daniel watched him carefully.

— You knew we would come?

— Not exactly.

Reed invited them inside.

— What happened twelve years ago was unfortunate.

— Unfortunate? — Clara repeated.

Reed looked at her.

— I chose my words carefully.

Daniel placed the photograph on the table.

— Do you recognize this?

Reed examined it.

His expression changed slightly.

— Arthur's study.

— And the clock?

— What about it?

— It had been moved.

Reed remained silent.

— Did you move it? — Daniel asked.

— No.

— Could you have?

Reed smiled faintly.

— Inspector, I could have done many things. That doesn't mean I did.

Daniel leaned forward.

— You would have benefited from Arthur's death.

The smile disappeared.

— That's an accusation.

— It's a fact.

— Perhaps.

Reed stood and walked toward the window.

— Arthur was going to expose the company's financial problems.

— Which would have ruined you.

— Yes.

Clara looked at him.

— So why didn't you kill him?

Reed turned around.

— Because I didn't need to.

Daniel frowned.

— Explain.

— Someone else was already doing it.

The room became silent.

— Who? — Daniel asked.

Reed shook his head.

— I never found out.

— You expect us to believe that?

— Believe whatever you want.

Daniel stood.

— You should have reported what you knew.

Reed looked at him.

— And you should have investigated the missing money twelve years ago.

Daniel said nothing.

Reed continued:

— If you had, Arthur might still be alive.

That night, Daniel returned to the old case file.

He read every page.

Then he noticed something.

The original investigator had written that Arthur's desk had been found unlocked.

But the photograph showed a key lying beside the lamp.

Daniel called Clara.

— Come to the station.

Twenty minutes later, she arrived.

— What did you find?

He showed her the photograph.

— The key.

— What about it?

— The report says the desk was locked.

Clara stared at the image.

— Then someone must have opened it.

— Exactly.

They checked the evidence inventory.

There was no record of a key being collected.

— Someone removed it from the scene — Clara said.

— Or someone took it before the evidence was documented.

They searched the old evidence storage system.

The key had never been logged.

Daniel sat back.

— So the person who entered the room knew where the key was.

Clara nodded.

— Someone close to Bell.

They returned to the Bell family's history.

Eventually, they discovered that Arthur had a daughter, Emily, who had been twenty-two at the time of his death.

She had left the country shortly afterward.

Daniel located her in another city.

When they finally spoke, Emily was reluctant to discuss her father.

— Why did you leave so quickly after his death? — Clara asked.

— Because I couldn't stay.

— Did you know about the financial problems?

Emily hesitated.

— Yes.

— Did you know about the missing money?

— Some of it.

Daniel placed the photograph on the table.

— Did you move the clock?

Emily stared at it.

Then she closed her eyes.

— Yes.

Clara exchanged a glance with Daniel.

— Why?

Emily took a long breath.

— Because my father wasn't alone that night.

Daniel leaned forward.

— Who was there?

— I don't know.

— You must have seen them.

— I saw someone leaving.

— Who?

Emily shook her head.

— It was dark.

Daniel waited.

— What did you do?

— I entered the study after they left. My father was already dead.

— And you moved the clock?

— I panicked.

— Why?

Emily looked at him.

— Because the clock was hiding something.

Daniel felt his attention sharpen.

— What?

— A small compartment in the wall.

— What was inside?

— Documents proving that someone had been stealing from my father for years.

Clara frowned.

— Why didn't you tell the police?

Emily looked down.

— Because I was afraid.

— Of whom?

She remained silent for several seconds.

Then she whispered:

— My brother.

Daniel froze.

Arthur Bell had never had a son.

At least, not officially.

The investigation took another week.

Eventually, they discovered that Arthur had indeed had a son from a previous relationship.

His name was Michael Bell.

He had changed his surname years earlier.

He had also worked for Arthur's company under a false identity.

Most importantly, he had access to the financial accounts.

Daniel found him in another country.

The evidence was finally sufficient to reconstruct what had happened.

Michael had been stealing from the company. Arthur had discovered the fraud and threatened to expose him. On the night of his death, Michael had confronted his father.

The argument had escalated.

Arthur had died.

Michael had then staged the scene to resemble suicide, moved the clock, and removed the documents that could have revealed the truth.

But he had not known that Emily had seen him leaving.

Daniel closed the case file.

Clara stood beside him.

— Twelve years.

— Yes.

— It should have been solved twelve years ago.

Daniel nodded.

— It should have.

Clara looked at the photograph.

— If someone had noticed the clock, we could have found the truth much earlier.

— If someone had investigated the missing key, we could have found it too.

She sighed.

— We would have solved it eventually.

Daniel shook his head.

— Maybe.

He looked at the old photograph one last time.

— But "eventually" isn't good enough when someone has been waiting twelve years for justice.

Clara nodded.

— You're right.

Daniel closed the folder.

The case had finally been solved.

But the satisfaction was incomplete.

The truth had survived not because the investigation had been perfect, but because one overlooked photograph had eventually found its way into the right hands.

Daniel stood up.

— Come on.

— Where are we going?

— To reopen another old case.

Clara smiled.

— You think we have another mistake to find?

Daniel picked up the photograph.

— There usually is.

And this time, he intended to look carefully.
